highlights:
Aven Cloud's on-demand GPU prices, adjusted continuously to supply and demand, set against the public on-demand list prices of the three largest public clouds — sourced, dated, and backed by a published price history, all on the same page.

Updated 2026-09-10 · 5 min read

The GPU Price Index tracks what a single GPU actually costs to rent. Every row combines Aven Cloud's live on-demand catalogue price — adjusted continuously to supply and demand — with the public on-demand list price published by each of the three largest public clouds for a comparable GPU. Nothing here is a quote or an estimate: the Aven Cloud side is the exact price you'd pay to order that GPU as of 14 November 2026, 07:59 UTC, and the reference side is a documented, dated list price (see Methodology below).

Per-second billing, no egress fees, release anytime.

Aven Cloud GPU Price Index

$1.84/GPU-hour

Simple average across GPUs currently available on demand, in USD per GPU-hour.

As of 14 November 2026, 07:59 UTC

### Methodology

Reference prices are the published on-demand list prices of the three largest public clouds: single-GPU instance where offered, otherwise the per-GPU share of the smallest instance carrying that GPU, largest US region, before any discount.

Checked 11 September 2026

...

Each row is one GPU model. On-demand is Aven Cloud's current single-GPU rate, adjusted continuously to supply and demand; spot is the interruptible rate for the same GPU where one is listed, and it can move on every refresh. Public cloud range is the low-to-high published on-demand list price for a comparable single-GPU instance across the three largest public clouds. Savings compares Aven Cloud's on-demand price with the high end of that range — the list price most buyers actually pay before any negotiated discount — and a short sparkline shows how Aven Cloud's own on-demand price has moved over time.

...

Aven Cloud's numbers come straight from the public catalogue API (`GET /v1/catalog`, documented at /docs) — the same endpoint the dashboard and every partner integration read from, so there is no separate marketing price list to fall out of sync. On-demand prices are adjusted continuously to supply and demand, and each catalogue entry carries a timestamp showing when its price last changed, shown above the table. Availability, the spot rate and the list of bookable configurations are live as well, and the index always reflects that snapshot: currently 306 bookable configurations from verified providers.

The public-cloud reference uses each of the three largest public clouds' own published on-demand list price for a comparable GPU: a genuine single-GPU instance where one exists, otherwise the per-GPU share of the smallest multi-GPU instance that carries it, in each provider's largest US region, before any negotiated or committed-use discount. Every reference figure is checked against the provider's own pricing page and dated; where a GPU is too new or too specialized for a clean like-for-like match, the index leaves that reference blank rather than guess.

The aggregate figure at the top of the table is a simple average of the 1-GPU on-demand prices available that day — not weighted by usage, and it can move when a GPU is added to or dropped from the comparison, not only when a price changes. List prices are also not the whole story on either side: a hyperscaler customer with a negotiated enterprise discount or reserved capacity may pay less than the list price shown here, just as an Aven Cloud spot price isn't directly comparable to an on-demand list price. Treat the index as a fair, sourced starting point — not the final word on any one contract.

Two things this index is not. It is not a live-ingested market feed: the public-cloud range is checked by hand on a monthly cadence and dated accordingly (see "Checked" above), so it moves in steps, not continuously. And it is not a long-run trend yet: price history for this index started on 9 September 2026, so the sparkline shown for each GPU will keep lengthening from a short starting series rather than reflect years of data.

results.title: Flopper Now Tracks GPU Rental Prices Across 24 Cloud Providers | Flopper.io
highlights:
Flopper Now Tracks GPU Rental Prices Across 24 Cloud Providers | Flopper.io

# Flopper Now Tracks GPU Rental Prices Across 24 Cloud Providers

337 per-GPU hourly rates from 24 clouds, refreshed every six hours, with price history back to July 2026. The spec database now tells you what each accelerator costs to rent, and who is cheapest today.

Published September 9, 2026 · Flopper.io Research

Flopper.io started as a specification database: peak TFLOPS by precision, memory, bandwidth and power for every datacenter GPU. Specs answer half of the buying question. The other half is price, and that number lives on 24 different pricing pages, in 24 different units. As of today, the pricing index collects 337 live listings from 24 GPU cloud providers, covering 89 GPUs, normalized to one unit: US dollars per GPU per hour. The pipeline refreshes every six hours and has recorded every price change since 14 July 2026, so each GPU page now carries a price history alongside its spec sheet.

## What the Same GPU Costs, Cloud to Cloud

The spread is the story. On the day of publication, an on-demand H100 SXM5 80 GB (2022) is listed by 16 providers, and the most expensive listing costs nearly seven times the cheapest. The B200 (2024) shows the same pattern with a three-fold gap across eight clouds. Some of that gap is real: interconnect, storage, support and region all cost money. Some of it is simply price discovery that has not happened yet, because nobody was lining the numbers up.

| GPU | Providers | Cheapest on-demand | Highest on-demand |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80 GB | 16 | $1.79/hr | $12.29/hr |
| NVIDIA A100 SXM4 80 GB | 11 | $1.40/hr | $4.10/hr |
| NVIDIA L40S 48 GB | 11 | $0.87/hr | $2.25/hr |
| NVIDIA H200 SXM 141 GB | 10 | $2.99/hr | $10.60/hr |
| NVIDIA B200 SXM 180 GB | 8 | $4.09/hr | $14.00/hr |
| NVIDIA B300 SXM 288 GB | 6 | $7.40/hr | $11.19/hr |
| AMD Instinct MI300X 192 GB | 5 | $2.39/hr | $6.00/hr |

On-demand, per-GPU, USD, as recorded on 9 September 2026. Spot, community and reserved listings are excluded from the range. Each GPU links to its live pricing page, which will have moved on by the time you read this.

## The 24 Providers

Coverage spans three kinds of seller. Hyperscale and general clouds publish rate cards: Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud, DigitalOcean, OVHcloud, Scaleway and Vultr. AI-first clouds, the neoclouds, sell the dense H100, H200 and Blackwell capacity that training runs need: CoreWeave, Lambda Labs, Nebius, Crusoe, DataCrunch, Hyperstack and their peers. Marketplaces, RunPod and Vast.ai, list third-party hosts and set the floor for most consumer and workstation parts.

| Provider | Live listings | GPUs priced |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RunPod | 78 | 42 |
| Vast.ai | 70 | 70 |
| Microsoft Azure | 25 | 9 |
| DataCrunch | 23 | 12 |
| CoreWeave | 18 | 10 |
| Hyperstack | 16 | 11 |
| DigitalOcean | 15 | 9 |
| Lambda Labs | 14 | 10 |
| Nebius | 12 | 6 |
| AceCloud | 9 | 9 |
| Paperspace | 8 | 6 |
| Massed Compute | 7 | 7 |
| Oracle Cloud (OCI) | 7 | 7 |
| Together AI | 6 | 3 |
| Crusoe | 6 | 6 |
| Scaleway | 5 | 5 |
| EcoHash | 4 | 1 |
| Cudo Compute | 3 | 3 |
| OVHcloud | 3 | 3 |
| Excess Supply | 2 | 2 |
| Denvr Dataworks | 2 | 1 |
| Vultr | 2 | 2 |
| Latitude.sh | 1 | 1 |
| Beyond.pl | 1 | 1 |

A listing is one GPU at one pricing type from one provider. Vast.ai and RunPod count high because their marketplaces publish hosts for consumer GPUs the dedicated clouds do not carry.

## How the Numbers Are Normalized

No two providers quote the same way. One prices an eight-GPU node, another a single accelerator, a third a monthly contract, and Scaleway prices in euros. Every listing goes through the same four steps before it reaches a page.

- Per GPU, per hour, in USD. Node prices are divided by the GPU count. Monthly rates are divided by 730 hours. Non-USD prices are converted at the live exchange rate on the day of the sync.
- Pricing types are kept apart. On-demand (191 listings), spot or preemptible (31), marketplace community hosts (111) and reserved commitments (4) never share a row. The headline cheapest price on each GPU page is always on-demand, so an interruptible instance cannot masquerade as the market rate.
- Every listing maps to one canonical part. A provider's "H100" is matched to the exact variant it sells, SXM5 or PCIe, 80 GB or 94 GB, so a PCIe price never dilutes the SXM figure. Names the matcher cannot place are logged and dropped rather than guessed.
- Bad data is quarantined, not published. A listing that lands far outside its GPU's price band is held back and flagged for review. Median, dispersion and FP8-per-dollar figures on the pricing index are calculated so that a single bad listing cannot move them.

...

## Price History, Not Just a Snapshot

A price comparison that only shows today cannot tell you whether $2.99 for an H200 is a bargain or the new normal. Since 14 July 2026 the pipeline has recorded 2,297 price points across 58 days and 101 GPUs, appending a row every time a listing changes. Each GPU pricing page plots the last 30 days with one line per provider, so you can see who cut, who held, and who quietly raised.

The index also reports a 30-day change per GPU. That figure compares the same providers' listings at both ends of the window, so a new cloud joining coverage registers as more data, not as a price move.

...

## What It Does Not Cover Yet

Public list prices only. Negotiated enterprise rates, reserved-capacity contracts and volume discounts are not published and are not tracked. Availability is shown where a provider publishes it, and a listed price does not guarantee capacity in the region you need. AWS and Google Cloud are the largest gaps in coverage; both publish pricing in formats that need heavier parsing and validation, and both are next on the list.

Confirm the live rate with the provider before committing. Some outbound links are affiliate links, which fund the pipeline and never change which provider appears cheapest.

results.title: CoreWeave pricing in 2026: every GPU rate explained
highlights:
Quick Answer

CoreWeave, a GPU cloud provider, prices start at $6.16 per GPU hour for an Nvidia H100 and reaches $8.60 for a B200, sold as fixed multi-GPU nodes: an 8x H100 node lists at $49.24 per hour on demand. Spot rates run up to 60 percent below on demand, reserved contracts discount up to 60 percent, and egress is free.

In April 2026, CoreWeave filed an 8-K with the SEC disclosing an expanded agreement with Meta: approximately $21 billion for AI cloud capacity through December 2032, deployed across multiple locations and including some of the first Nvidia Vera Rubin systems, per the filing.

...

## How much does CoreWeave cost in 2026?

On-demand GPU nodes run from $10.00 per hour for an 8x L40 to $68.80 for an 8x B200, with the workhorse 8x H100 node at $49.24. Every figure on the public card prices a full instance, not a chip, so the CoreWeave price you’ll actually compare against other clouds takes one extra division.

Here are CoreWeave’s North America rates as of 2026, normalized per GPU:

| GPU (instance config) | On demand, node/hr | Per GPU/hr | Spot, node/hr | Inference single GPU/hr |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nvidia HGX H100 (8x) | $49.24 | $6.16 | $19.71 | $6.16 |
| Nvidia HGX H200 (8x) | $50.44 | $6.31 | $20.93 | $6.31 |
| Nvidia HGX B200 (8x) | $68.80 | $8.60 | $34.11 | $8.60 |
| Nvidia GB200 NVL72 (4 GPU) | $42.00 | $10.50 | N/A | $10.50 |
| Nvidia HGX B300 (8x) | Contact sales | N/A | $35.84 | N/A |
| Nvidia GB300 NVL72 (4 GPU) | Contact sales | N/A | N/A | N/A |
| Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, high memory (8x) | $20.00 | $2.50 | $11.09 | $2.50 |
| Nvidia GH200 (1x) | $6.50 | $6.50 | N/A | $6.50 |
| Nvidia A100 80GB (8x) | $21.60 | $2.70 | $9.65 | $2.70 |
| Nvidia L40S (8x) | $18.00 | $2.25 | $7.88 | $2.25 |
| Nvidia L40 (8x) | $10.00 | $1.25 | $6.27 | $1.25 |

Note: GB200 and GB300 instances bundle two Grace Blackwell Superchips, four GPUs total. The inference column applies only to CoreWeave inference platform customers. European spot rates differ slightly: the H100 node runs $19.51 there versus $19.71 in North America.

...

You can buy CoreWeave compute three ways: on demand by the hour, spot at up to 60 percent off with interruption risk, and reserved capacity under negotiated multi-year contracts discounted up to 60 percent. The rate card shows the first two. The CoreWeave business model runs on the third.

...

What utilization does to CoreWeave’s on-demand rates, in CloudZero’s arithmetic:

| Cluster utilization | H100, effective per GPU/hr | H200 | B200 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 100% (list rate) | $6.16 | $6.31 | $8.60 |
| 75% | $8.21 | $8.41 | $11.47 |
| 50% | $12.32 | $12.62 | $17.20 |
| 35% | $17.60 | $18.03 | $24.57 |

The comparison lands hard: a half-utilized H100 node on CoreWeave costs more per useful hour than a fully utilized B200. Most teams comparing providers argue about a dollar of list-rate difference while a multiple of that leaks through idle capacity, a pattern CloudZero sees constantly in GPU workload spend.

...

## What changed in 2026

Blackwell landed on the public rate card. The 8x B200 node lists at $68.80 per hour with an $8.60 single GPU inference rate, the GB200 NVL72 instance at $42.00, and B300-class hardware shows spot pricing while on-demand buyers still go through sales, the usual tell for supply-constrained chips.

The contracts got longer and stranger. Meta’s expansion to approximately $21 billion runs through December 2032. Nvidia itself agreed to backstop CoreWeave in a deal reported at $6.3 billion, guaranteeing it will buy any unsold capacity, per CoreWeave’s own SEC 8-K filing on the order. That’s Nvidia underwriting demand for the same chips it sells CoreWeave, a hedge most buyers negotiating capacity elsewhere don’t get.

And the H100 price per hour conversation started aging. With H200 nodes at a 2.4 percent premium over H100 and Blackwell now orderable, 2026 budget cycles are the first where the chip generation decision comes before the provider decision.

results.title: Alpha AI relaunches compute terminal for GPU pricing and power data By Investing.com
highlights:
Published Sep 09, 2026, 08:36 a.m.

Alpha AI Corporation announced the relaunch of its Alpha Liquid Terminal platform as the ALT/X Compute Terminal, shifting the product’s focus to pricing, power, and capacity data for the global AI compute market, according to a press release dated Sept. 9, 2026.

The relaunch follows investments made by Alpha Compute Corp. (Nasdaq: ALP) in both Alpha Liquid Terminal and its parent company, Alpha AI Corporation, the first of which was announced Dec. 16, 2025.

The first public release of the platform includes a compute screener that allows users to compare GPU capacity across providers and regions. The screener covers hardware including Nvidia H100, H200, B200, and B300-class accelerators, with filters for pricing structure, region, and availability. Pricing types covered include on-demand, spot, reserved, and multi-year contracted rates, normalized to a per-GPU-hour basis.

The platform also includes a power and energy data layer covering industrial electricity rates, grid carbon mix, renewable sourcing, and cooling efficiency benchmarks by region. A data center tracking feature covers announced, under-construction, and operational facilities, including operator details and power profiles.

An AI assistant called ChatAnalyst for compute is included, allowing users to query pricing spreads, regional cost differentials, and capacity data in natural language.

Planned additions include expanded provider coverage, historical pricing time series, forward and contract curves, and an API for institutional users. The company also stated that its ALTX token utility framework, which includes pay-as-you-go access and staking for premium data tiers, is being adapted to the compute dataset.

Alpha AI Corporation stated that the ALT/X Compute Terminal operates as a vendor-neutral platform and does not preference Alpha Compute Corp. capacity in its screener results. Alpha Compute Corp. is described as an investor in the platform, not its operator.

SMM 9月9日讯：

H200：SXM整机买断价单月连涨三档 月租需求端破14万

SMM获悉，H200 SXM版本整机买断价近一个月呈连续小幅上行——8月24日某渠道256台H200现货报535万元/台（含13%税，深圳仓），9月1日多渠道报价上沿推至540万元，9月4日深圳一手2T整机全新提货价报到545万元/台，单月含税口径累计上移约10万元。SMM获悉，月租端本月同步走强：8月初某运营商128台HGX版本月租12万元、8月中旬华东32台HGX八卡模组报12.8万元三年闭口，9月4日江苏某机房30台新上架需求端已报到13万至14万元/台·月，需求方报价带整体上移至12.8万至14万区间。值得注意的是，8月底业内反馈H200整机已在535万至540万元区间横盘约10天、买方多选择观望，本轮上行后观望情绪进一步固化。

SMM获悉，华东地区10台H100整机在一个半月内分三批出清，成交价由首批2台的7.8万元/台·月升至次批4台的8.0万元、末批4台达8.5万元，累计上涨9%、加权均价8.16万元，已突破此前主流报价区间7.5万—8.2万元/台·月上沿。SMM获悉，受大模型训练与推理需求双重拉动，华北环京区域H100租赁报价已迫近9万元/台·月，较华东末批再高约5000元。同一批次资源分批放货、逐批提价，放货节奏本身正成为价格发现的主要方式。

线上市场：H100模组现询价+中小批量需求+5090变现出货

SMM今日下午自线上渠道直接采集到三条独立市场信号：下午1时40分左右，某渠道明示"收H100模组，有现货的来报价"，以"模组"而非整机为采购单位，指向 H100 月租报8.5 万元新高的下游补货需求；下午 4 时 20 分至 40 分，某需求方提出4 台 H100 + 4 台 H200 的小批量租赁配置，与 H200 月租破 14 万、H100 月租迫近 9 万的趋势呼应，市场已不止单批百台级大单、4 台级即时需求同步冒头；下午 1 时 44 分，某渠道以"变现"口吻集中出货 5090 涡轮卡 200 张，"变现"二字反映该机型价格在月内已上移至含税 4.3 万附近后部分玩家兑现利润的意愿增强。

SMM分析： 今日市场主线是高端算力租赁端的集体破位。H200买断价在一个月内含税口径累计上移约10万元、月租需求端报价带同步上移至12.8万—14万区间，价格上行与买方观望同步出现，卖方定价权增强与买方接受度承压的拉锯持续。H100同期在华东分批放货节奏下逐批提价创8.5万元新高、华北环京受训练与推理双重需求拉动报价迫近9万关口。国产端，运营商首单交付节点从9月延至四季度、Atlas 300V 整机2500元月租将国产算力价格谱系下探至三千元以下，国产替代路径上的产能瓶颈与场景分层并行显现。下午线上信号与上午主线形成三类呼应：H100 模组补货指向月租新高向下游硬件传导；4 台级小批量需求方现身印证 H100/H200 租赁端的需求分层；5090 涡轮 200 张以"变现"集中出货则反映中端机型价格在月内上行后兑现利润的实操路径。

results.title: GPU Pricing Splits as Spot Rates Triple and Capacity Goes to Auction — TechReaderDaily
highlights:
Spot GPU rental rates tripled in Nebius Group's Q2 2026 results while a new auction market is trying to put a real number on reserved GPU capacity.

...

GPU spot rental rates tripled. That opening figure came out of Nebius Group's Q2 2026 earnings call on August 12, 2026, as reported by Morningstar. The unit is worth holding still: a spot rate is the price of a GPU-hour on a short horizon, clearing against scarcity in the moment rather than against a multi-month reservation. In an industry that publicly prices capacity in gigawatts and privately prices contracts in months, a tripled spot rate is the single number that repriced the room without anyone having to renegotiate a thing.

Five days earlier, the other side of the market started moving. On August 4, Fluence launched GPU Cluster Auctions, a marketplace for reserved GPU capacity that lets AI teams run competitive bids for clusters instead of accepting a posted term sheet. Reuters carried the announcement. Spot capacity reprices too fast. Reserved capacity reprices too slowly. An auction is the attempt to make the slow side produce a number.

> GPU spot rental rates continue to climb as the artificial intelligence supply/demand imbalance intensifies and neoclouds want to maximize value extracted from short-term pricing. Morningstar, August 12, 2026

The second clause of that sentence is the analytical center. The neoclouds were not framed as cost-passing utilities. Morningstar used the word maximize. For a buyer, that changes the negotiating position. The seller is a market maker monetizing a supply gap, not a capacity landlord collecting a fixed margin. The behavior matches the pricing: short-term scarcity is the product, and the spot book is where it gets marked to market.

The retail channel shows the same appetite in raw dollars. Gaming GPU prices rose as much as 41 percent between June and August 2026, according to MSN, and the sellers did not suffer. PC Partner Group, the Hong Kong-listed parent of Zotac, Inno3D, and Manli, reported on August 14 that its net profit doubled. TechSpot tracked prices across 10 countries and found GeForce cards taking the biggest hit. The margin did not leak to discounters; it stayed in the vendor ledger.

...

In cloud, Morningstar's note frames the neocloud as the party that maximizes

...

A secondary market is forming alongside the primary one. In July, Yahoo Finance reported that Compute Exchange launched a secondary GPU marketplace as H100 and A100 demand held. Secondary trading appears when primary allocation is rationed and trust in posted prices cracks. It also raises a question the primary contracts have barely touched: who carries the risk when a reserved cluster changes hands, and at what discount to the original term.

The procurement menu now shows three prices. Spot rental rates tripled in Nebius's Q2 call. Reserved capacity is moving toward auction clearing. Retail cards stood 40 percent above their old street prices on Newegg over the summer, per PCGamesN, and the entry tier is expected to tighten again. A team that anchors to any one of those numbers is running a single-source pricing model in a market that has stopped behaving like one.

...

Cloud spot prices are per GPU-hour, a rental. Reserved auctions clear per cluster per month. These are not three views of one price; they are three instruments with different risk profiles. None converts cleanly to another without an assumption about utilization, useful life, and financing cost. The first slide any analyst should show is the conversion table, and it has not appeared.
